promptText: Some argue governments should ban private cars in city centres to reduce pollution. Others believe individuals should have the right to drive wherever they wish. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The systemic regulation of private automotive access within urban centres.
distractors: The mitigation of vehicle emissions throughout the industrialised world.
The comparative efficiency of public transport and the private motor car.
The redesign of congested cities to eliminate persistent traffic jams.

phases.correct: The urgent necessity of mitigating vehicle-induced environmental degradation.
distractors: The immediate prohibition of private vehicles from all city centres.
The construction of wider arterial roads to relieve chronic congestion.
The provision of safer routes for pedestrians and cyclists downtown.

phases.correct: sharply reducing localised tailpipe emissions in densely populated districts
distractors: eliminating tailpipe emissions altogether by mandating electric vehicles
criminalising vehicle ownership for anyone residing in a city centre
obliging every commuter to walk or cycle to their place of employment

phases.correct: Comprehensive bans on combustion engines in designated downtown districts.
distractors: Municipal pledges to halve urban air pollution levels within the coming decade.
The demolition of inner-city roads to create parkland and public squares.
The free distribution of bicycles to every registered resident of a city.

phases.correct: an outright ban abandons commuters for whom no transit alternative exists
distractors: unrestricted driving inevitably produces gridlock and hazardous air quality
the resulting fall in emissions would be offset within a decade by rising freight traffic
vehicle emissions remain the gravest single threat to public health in cities

phases.correct: The preservation of individual freedom of movement and choice.
distractors: The economic burden that vehicle restrictions impose upon motorists.
The continued profitability of the domestic automotive industry.
The convenience of the private car for households with several young children.

phases.correct: safeguarding the autonomy of citizens to traverse urban space unimpeded by the state
distractors: sparing motorists the expense and chronic unreliability of scheduled public transport services
permitting drivers to disregard environmental regulation whenever time is short
guaranteeing every motorist a parking space at no cost in the city centre

phases.correct: Unrestricted access to central districts by way of the public road network.
distractors: Road-pricing schemes that charge motorists for entering the city centre.
Multi-storey car parks constructed on every block of the central commercial district.
The withdrawal of bus services so that residents are compelled to drive.

phases.correct: unchecked vehicular freedom generates compounding gridlock and toxic air
distractors: an outright prohibition strands those with no realistic alternative route
private motoring is already beyond the means of most urban households
commuters who drive everywhere tend to suffer poorer cardiovascular health over time

phases.correct: municipalities must invest in mass transit while phasing out high-emission vehicles
distractors: cities should restrict the most polluting vehicles at peak hours and leave the remainder untouched
governments ought to ban private cars and allow citizens to make their own arrangements
the right to drive should be absolute provided motorists pay an environmental levy

phases.correct: sound urban policy must reconcile ecological protection with essential public mobility
distractors: restricting traffic delivers cleaner air and a more attractive city centre
public transport is invariably cheaper for the commuter than the running of a private car
citizens will never voluntarily surrender the convenience of the private vehicle

promptText: Some say governments should fund only university science degrees because they are the most useful. Others believe public money should continue to support arts subjects. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The allocation of state funding across university disciplines.
distractors: The comparative economic utility of scientific and artistic fields of study.
The escalating tuition fees confronting contemporary undergraduates.
The difficulty of persuading school leavers to enter technical fields.

phases.correct: The prioritisation of STEM disciplines to drive technological advancement.
distractors: The superior employment prospects enjoyed by graduates of the sciences.
The redirection of all humanities funding towards laboratory-based departments.
The expense of maintaining well-equipped research laboratories.

phases.correct: channelling resources into disciplines that yield measurable industrial return
distractors: directing school leavers towards the degrees industry currently demands
obliging science graduates to work for the state that financed them
doubling the tuition fees payable by students of the creative arts and humanities

phases.correct: Full subsidy for degrees in medical research, software engineering and applied physics.
distractors: National strategies that identify science as a driver of future prosperity.
Universities allocating their newest buildings exclusively to the sciences.
Mathematics being made a compulsory subject for every undergraduate.

phases.correct: an exclusive focus on technical skill neglects the ethical judgement required to govern innovation
distractors: scientific research is costly and delivers returns only over the very long term
laboratory disciplines already attract the greater share of private investment
many science graduates ultimately pursue careers outside their field of study

phases.correct: The continued public financing of the humanities and creative disciplines.
distractors: The cultural impoverishment that follows the neglect of the arts.
The obligation of science students to study poetry before graduating.
The payment of a state salary to practising artists and musicians.

phases.correct: fostering cultural preservation, communication and sociopolitical analysis
distractors: cultivating the creative industries that generate substantial export revenue for the nation
ensuring that national museums acquire sufficient works to attract visitors
allowing students to select subjects that place them under less pressure

phases.correct: Public grants for academic programmes in history and literature.
distractors: Government subsidy of the film, publishing and design industries.
Free concert and theatre tickets distributed to all enrolled undergraduates.
Monumental public sculpture commissioned for every major city centre.

phases.correct: unrestricted arts funding can produce a workforce misaligned with economic demand
distractors: the cultural benefits of arts funding cannot readily be quantified by government
humanities faculties are considerably cheaper to run than scientific ones
sustained reading of literature has declined sharply since the arrival of the internet

phases.correct: the state must chiefly subsidise high-yield STEM sectors while preserving targeted arts funding
distractors: public money should follow whichever disciplines students themselves elect to study at admission
governments ought to fund science generously and leave the arts to private philanthropy
every degree should be funded equally because all knowledge is of comparable worth

phases.correct: a resilient society needs both the capacity to innovate and the wisdom to govern innovation
distractors: scientific and artistic disciplines each contribute something valuable to a nation
technological advance is the only reliable route to sustained national prosperity and influence
universities are best placed to determine how their own funding is distributed

promptText: Some believe prisons exist strictly to punish those who break the law. Others argue they should concentrate entirely on reforming offenders. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The fundamental purpose of the modern penal system.
distractors: The effectiveness of imprisonment as a general deterrent.
The social conditions that give rise to criminality.
The escalating cost of housing convicted offenders.

phases.correct: The prioritisation of punishment for legal transgression.
distractors: The moral claim of victims to see wrongdoing answered.
The deliberate maintenance of austere conditions within prisons.
The restoration of capital punishment for grave offences.

phases.correct: depriving offenders of liberty as the direct consequence of their own conduct
distractors: ensuring that the severity of a sentence corresponds to the gravity of the offence
compelling inmates to perform unpaid labour in repayment of their debt to society
publicising convictions widely so that potential offenders are shamed into compliance

phases.correct: Mandatory custodial sentences imposed for severe or repeated offences.
distractors: Sentencing guidelines that remove judicial discretion from the courts entirely.
Extended periods of solitary confinement for the most serious criminals.
The permanent withdrawal of family visiting rights from all inmates.

phases.correct: a strictly punitive model yields high reoffending among those eventually released
distractors: custodial sentences remove dangerous individuals from the community altogether
the expense of prolonged imprisonment falls ultimately upon the law-abiding taxpayer
offenders subjected to harsh regimes become more determined to escape them

phases.correct: The prioritisation of rehabilitation and psychological reform.
distractors: The treatment of offenders as products of social disadvantage.
The provision of comfortable accommodation for every inmate.
The early release of prisoners who express sincere and lasting remorse.

phases.correct: equipping inmates with vocational training and therapy that addresses the roots of offending
distractors: offering inmates the education and support they were denied in childhood
prescribing medication to offenders whose behaviour cannot otherwise be managed
occupying prisoners with organised sport so that idleness does not breed trouble

phases.correct: In-prison education programmes and substance-abuse counselling services.
distractors: Supervised release schemes for inmates nearing the end of a term.
Weekend home leave granted to prisoners of good behaviour.
Fully funded university degrees awarded to every serving inmate.

phases.correct: an exclusively rehabilitative approach denies victims justice and erodes the deterrent force of law
distractors: a purely punitive regime releases offenders who remain disposed to offend again
therapeutic provision requires staff and funding that prison services rarely possess
offenders who complete vocational training reoffend at considerably lower rates

phases.correct: the penal system must combine deprivation of liberty with compulsory rehabilitation
distractors: prisons should punish serious offenders and rehabilitate only those convicted of lesser crimes
custodial sentences ought to be replaced by mandatory therapeutic programmes
society should concentrate on preventing crime, rendering the prison largely redundant

phases.correct: protecting society demands both the containment of danger and a fall in reoffending
distractors: a prison that neither punishes nor reforms serves no purpose whatsoever
indefinite imprisonment imposes a cost no national treasury can realistically sustain
every offender can be restored to society given sufficient counselling and time

promptText: Many believe that working from home benefits employees and companies alike. Others think it isolates staff and lowers overall productivity. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The organisational shift toward decentralised, remote working models.
distractors: The measurable productivity of employees working outside the office.
The falling commercial demand for office space in major cities.
The technologies that permit dispersed teams to collaborate.

phases.correct: The mutual benefit of remote work for employee and organisation alike.
distractors: The savings that accrue to employers who relinquish costly office premises.
The improved work-life balance reported by home-based employees.
The obligation of every firm to permit staff to work remotely.

phases.correct: eliminating commuting time and overhead cost, thus raising autonomy and efficiency
distractors: returning to employees the hours formerly surrendered to the daily commute
permitting staff to determine their own working hours without any managerial oversight
transferring the cost of equipment and utilities from employer to employee

phases.correct: Distributed firms reporting reduced property costs and improved retention.
distractors: Employers reporting that remote staff are happier than office-based staff.
Companies relocating their headquarters to smaller and cheaper premises.
Staff attending departmental meetings by video from home several times each week.

phases.correct: unstructured remote work dissolves the work-life boundary and invites burnout
distractors: dispersed teams gradually lose the cohesion on which genuine collaboration depends
remote arrangements return several unpaid commuting hours to the employee
home working suits only those roles that can be performed on a computer

phases.correct: The damage done to collaborative capacity and psychological wellbeing.
distractors: The difficulty of supervising employees who cannot be observed directly.
The loneliness reported by staff who work alone for extended periods at home.
The impossibility of performing most occupations outside a workplace.

phases.correct: eroding spontaneous contact and fragmenting the cohesion of working teams
distractors: depriving junior employees of the informal mentoring an office provides
exposing organisations to the failure of domestic internet connections
allowing staff to disregard instructions they would not question in a shared office

phases.correct: Delayed projects arising from asynchronous communication and staff isolation.
distractors: Reduced innovation in firms whose employees no longer meet one another in person.
New recruits resigning within months of joining a dispersed organisation.
Employees attending to domestic responsibilities during working hours.

phases.correct: falling output usually reflects poor digital management rather than remote work itself
distractors: the isolation reported by remote staff diminishes as they grow accustomed to it
office environments impose constant interruptions that depress concentration just as severely
the difficulty is generational and will resolve itself as the workforce changes

phases.correct: firms should adopt hybrid models pairing remote flexibility with purposeful in-person collaboration
distractors: organisations should permit remote work for tasks that require sustained concentration
employers ought to require attendance at the office in order to protect productivity
staff should be free to decide each morning whether or not to attend the workplace

phases.correct: a hybrid arrangement maximises efficiency while protecting the wellbeing and creativity of staff
distractors: flexibility and collaboration are both indispensable to a modern organisation
employees will resign in numbers if compelled to attend an office five days each week
the office has become an expensive relic of an earlier and more industrial era

promptText: Some parents firmly restrict their children's screen time to protect healthy development. Others insist digital devices are essential for modern learning and should not be limited. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The regulation of children's exposure to digital technology.
distractors: The developmental harm attributed to prolonged childhood screen use.
The age at which a child should be given a smartphone.
The influence of social media upon adolescent behaviour.

phases.correct: The imposition of firm limits to safeguard physiological and cognitive growth.
distractors: The withdrawal of electronic devices until a child reaches adulthood.
The damage that extended screen use inflicts upon developing eyesight.
The preference of many parents for books over electronic entertainment.

phases.correct: preventing sedentary habit and limiting the effect of overstimulation on developing attention
distractors: restricting the hours a child may spend seated before an illuminated screen each day
supervising the material a child encounters when using the internet unattended at home
ensuring that homework is fully completed before any recreational device is permitted

phases.correct: Household rules barring all tablet use on school days in favour of outdoor play.
distractors: Parental controls that restrict a child's device to educational applications.
The removal of every entertainment application from a child's telephone.
Schools prohibiting computers from the classroom in all circumstances.

phases.correct: draconian restriction breeds digital illiteracy and social exclusion among peers
distractors: unmediated access degenerates into passive consumption rather than active learning
children denied devices at home will simply borrow them from classmates and neighbours
rules of this kind provoke resentment and damage the parental relationship

phases.correct: The integration of unrestricted digital access into contemporary education.
distractors: The technological fluency that early exposure to devices confers.
The role of the tablet in occupying a child during a parent's working day.
The belief that educational software will eventually replace the classroom teacher.

phases.correct: equipping the young with technological fluency and access to global information
distractors: familiarising children with the devices and platforms their future employment will demand
allowing pupils to pursue their own interests without a teacher's constant direction
teaching young people to repair and maintain their own devices and equipment

phases.correct: Immersive software teaching coding or language through gamified interaction.
distractors: Online encyclopaedias that place a vast library within a child's reach.
Video platforms on which children encounter some occasional educational material.
Calculator applications that complete a pupil's mathematics homework.

phases.correct: unmediated access commonly degenerates into passive consumption rather than engagement
distractors: strict limits leave a child unable to use the tools their schooling assumes
few families can afford a separate device for every child in the household
devices persistently distract pupils from the lessons their teachers are attempting to deliver

phases.correct: caregivers must move from limiting screen time to curating its content and purpose
distractors: parents should permit devices freely for schoolwork and restrict them for entertainment
screen time ought to be forbidden on weekdays and allowed freely at weekends
children should use computers under supervision at school but never at home

phases.correct: preparing the young for a digitised future means harnessing utility without dependency
distractors: the value of a device depends entirely upon the purpose to which it is put
technological competence is now a prerequisite for almost every occupation and profession
children invariably lose interest in screens once other pursuits are offered

promptText: Some think international tourism strengthens the local economy. Others argue it erodes local cultures and harms the natural environment. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The socioeconomic and ecological consequences of international tourism.
distractors: The enrichment of host economies through sustained foreign visitor spending.
The environmental damage inflicted by mass air travel across the globe.
The declining affordability of overseas holidays for ordinary households.

phases.correct: The economic revitalisation generated by foreign visitor expenditure.
distractors: The channelling of external capital into local infrastructure projects.
The construction of airports and motorways to accommodate rising arrivals.
The seasonal fluctuation of income within tourism-dependent economies.

phases.correct: channelling external capital into local service industries and public infrastructure
distractors: financing local schools and clinics from levies imposed upon arriving visitors
attracting multinational hotel chains that displace locally owned businesses
compelling national governments to liberalise their visa regimes for foreign arrivals

phases.correct: Coastal regions financing clinics and schools through visitor levies.
distractors: Island states deriving the greater part of their national income from arrivals.
Airlines expanding their long-haul networks to serve emerging destinations.
Resort developments purchased outright by overseas investment consortia.

phases.correct: much tourist revenue is repatriated by foreign-owned operators, leaving host communities a fraction of the declared profit
distractors: visitor demand frequently supplies the funding and political will that conservation of these sites requires

phases.correct: The erosion of indigenous culture and the degradation of fragile ecosystems.
distractors: The staging of inherited tradition as spectacle for paying visitors.
The strain that seasonal crowding places upon municipal services.
The dependence of host regions upon a single volatile industry.

phases.correct: commodifying authentic tradition into staged performance while overburdening finite natural resources
distractors: eradicating every trace of indigenous practice wherever visitors arrive in number
displacing residential housing stock with short-term lettings priced for visitors
exposing younger residents to consumer habits imported from wealthier societies

phases.correct: Bleached reef systems and heritage quarters converted into souvenir arcades.
distractors: Ancient monuments restored with revenue drawn from admission charges.
Historic city centres whose residents have been displaced by holiday lettings.
Coastal footpaths eroded by the passage of guided walking parties.

phases.correct: visitor demand often supplies the funding and political incentive that conservation itself requires
distractors: much of the declared revenue never reaches the communities that actually host the visitors

phases.correct: states should pursue capacity-limited tourism that reinvests visitor revenue in cultural and habitat protection
distractors: host states should restrict arrivals wherever heritage or habitat is at risk, whatever the cost to local livelihoods

phases.correct: prosperity drawn from a destination's distinctiveness is self-defeating unless that distinctiveness is protected
distractors: the economic gains of international tourism outweigh its cultural and environmental costs over time
communities cannot be expected to surrender their inherited way of life merely to secure foreign currency earnings
unregulated growth in any industry eventually exhausts the very resource upon which it depends

promptText: Some argue that government spending on space is wasteful and should be redirected to problems on Earth. Others believe space research delivers vital technological progress. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The justification of public expenditure on extraterrestrial exploration.
distractors: The diversion of state research budgets away from pressing terrestrial needs.
The commercial viability of privately financed spaceflight ventures.
The scientific value of a continued human presence in low Earth orbit.

phases.correct: The redirection of aerospace budgets to humanitarian priorities.
distractors: The reallocation of finite public capital to immediate social crises.
The permanent closure of every national space agency in the developed world.

phases.correct: reallocating finite public capital to immediate crises such as poverty and disease
distractors: abolishing national space agencies outright so that their budgets may be spent at home
prioritising expenditure whose benefits accrue to the present generation
transferring engineering expertise from orbital projects into domestic infrastructure work

phases.correct: National budgets diverting orbital funding into housing and disease eradication.
distractors: Governments postponing planned lunar missions during periods of economic contraction.
Charitable foundations financing vaccination campaigns in low-income states.
Legislatures capping the annual budgets of national aerospace agencies.

phases.correct: space budgets are a marginal fraction of national expenditure, so abolishing them would resolve little
distractors: the same innovations could plausibly be pursued more cheaply through research conducted on Earth

phases.correct: The technological dividend yielded by sustained astronautical research.
distractors: The pressure to innovate that extreme operating conditions impose.
The strategic advantage conferred by an independent launch capability.
The international collaboration fostered by jointly operated orbital laboratories.

phases.correct: compelling innovation under extreme constraint, yielding technologies that migrate into civilian use
distractors: producing the satellite networks upon which global navigation, weather forecasting and broadcasting depend

phases.correct: Satellite navigation, water purification and medical imaging derived from orbital research.
distractors: Improved weather forecasting made possible by internationally shared launch capacity.
Materials science advanced through experiments conducted in microgravity.
Telecommunications networks maintained by commercially operated satellites.

phases.correct: comparable innovations might plausibly have been achieved through targeted terrestrial research at far lower cost
distractors: the sums involved remain trivial when set beside the totality of annual public expenditure

phases.correct: governments should sustain a modest, outcome-driven space programme while the bulk of public funds addresses immediate social need
distractors: states should fund space science and social welfare in equal measure, since both serve the public interest
space exploration should be surrendered entirely to private enterprise, with the state confining itself to regulation

phases.correct: long-horizon scientific capacity and immediate humanitarian obligation are complementary rather than competing claims

promptText: Some think heavy taxes should be imposed on fast food to improve public health. Others believe people should be entirely free to choose what they eat. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The legitimacy of state fiscal intervention in individual dietary choice.

The regulation of advertising by the processed food industry.

phases.correct: The imposition of punitive duties in order to improve population health.
distractors: The raising of retail prices until consumption patterns shift.
The recovery of healthcare costs from the industry responsible.
The exclusion of fast-food outlets from areas near schools.

distractors: pricing processed food beyond the reach of ordinary consumers so that demand for it disappears altogether
generating revenue that may be directed towards the treatment of diet-related illness
signalling official disapproval of products the state considers harmful to health

distractors: dietary preference is conditioned from childhood by industrial marketing rather than freely formed

phases.correct: The preservation of individual autonomy over personal consumption.
distractors: The restriction of the state to informing rather than coercing consumers.

phases.correct: leaving the state to inform rather than compel, so that authority over the body remains with the individual
distractors: removing fiscal obstacles altogether so that consumers may eat precisely as they choose to eat

phases.correct: Transparent nutritional labelling and public campaigns that inform choice.
distractors: Voluntary agreements under which manufacturers reduce sugar content.

phases.correct: genuine autonomy presupposes an informed chooser, yet preference is conditioned from childhood by marketing
distractors: the burden of any such duty falls hardest upon precisely those households least able to afford an alternative

distractors: governments should impose duties upon all fast food and leave consumers to adjust their spending

promptText: Some believe printed newspapers will be completely replaced by online news. Others argue that print media will always keep a valued place in society. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The supersession of the physical newspaper by digital distribution.

phases.correct: digital migration has severed the revenue model that funded investigative reporting, yielding many platforms and little original journalism

phases.correct: The enduring civic and material value of the printed edition.

phases.correct: print will persist as a curated, premium and local format while digital assumes immediate reporting

promptText: Some think testing medical products on animals is justified because it saves human lives. Others argue it is cruel and needless now that modern alternatives exist. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: these technologies cannot yet model systemic interaction across an organism, so full substitution is unavailable
distractors: species difference already renders a great deal of animal data an unreliable guide to human response

phases.correct: regulators should mandate validated alternatives where they exist and confine animal use to questions no technology can answer
distractors: animal experimentation ought to be prohibited outright the moment any alternative method becomes commercially available for research use
researchers themselves should be trusted to select whichever method yields the most reliable evidence available

phases.correct: an ethical framework minimises suffering to the least quantity current science requires, revising that threshold as science advances
distractors: the suffering of laboratory animals is outweighed by the human lives that medical research ultimately saves
no defensible ethics permits the infliction of avoidable suffering once a reliable alternative has been demonstrated to work in practice

promptText: Some argue that competitive sport teaches children discipline and resilience. Others believe competition breeds needless stress and that youth sport should simply be fun. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The place of competitive structures in the sporting development of children.
distractors: The psychological toll that organised sport exacts upon its youngest participants.
The comparative merits of team sports and individual athletic pursuits.
The decline of physical activity among children in the developed world.

phases.correct: The cultivation of discipline and resilience through structured competition.
distractors: The enjoyment and social pleasure that unpressured play affords the young.
The physical fitness that regular athletic training confers upon growing children.
The identification of exceptional talent at the earliest possible age.

phases.correct: exposing children to consequential failure within a supervised environment
distractors: subjecting children to comparison at a stage when identity is still forming
rewarding the most gifted competitors with places in representative teams
instilling obedience to the coach through the discipline of daily training routines

phases.correct: School leagues in which regular defeats are followed by coaching and measurable improvement.
distractors: Elite academies that select the most promising nine-year-olds and train them to professional standards.
Physical education lessons in which every pupil receives an identical participation award.
Weekend athletics clubs organised entirely by parents rather than by qualified coaches.

phases.correct: resilience develops only where failure is reframed constructively rather than punished
distractors: the distress attributed to sport originates in adult conduct rather than in competition
children who lose repeatedly will in time abandon the sport however sensitively they are coached
competitive sport delivers its benefits only to those children who possess natural ability

phases.correct: The psychological burden imposed upon children by premature competitive pressure.
distractors: The character said to be formed by learning to accept defeat with composure.
The physical injuries sustained through excessive training in early adolescence.
The erosion of unstructured play as organised fixtures colonise the leisure of the young.

phases.correct: tethering a child's self-worth to comparative ranking while identity is still forming
distractors: confronting children with consequential defeat before they possess the means to interpret it
obliging young athletes to train at hours that encroach upon sleep and study
concentrating coaching resources upon the few children already deemed talented

phases.correct: High dropout rates among adolescents in early-selection systems, linked to performance anxiety.
distractors: Talented young players discarded by academies before they reach the age of sixteen.
Adolescent athletes presenting with disordered eating and chronic overuse injuries in weight-graded sports.
Parents pursuing coaches and clubs through the courts over disputed selection decisions.

phases.correct: the distress is traceable to adult conduct and selection design rather than to competition itself
distractors: competitive pressure is harmful chiefly to those children who lack athletic aptitude
many adolescents leave sport because of academic workload rather than because of pressure
non-competitive programmes struggle to retain the interest of older adolescents

phases.correct: youth sport should retain competition but organise it around mastery, so that improvement rather than ranking defines success
distractors: competition should be deferred until adolescence, once a young person's sense of identity has settled
schools should abolish league tables and trophies so that participation alone is recognised and rewarded
children should be free to choose between competitive squads and purely recreational sessions at school

phases.correct: the formative value of sport lies in how competition is framed by adults, not in its presence or absence
distractors: competition is beneficial provided that adults refrain from imposing their own ambitions
children who learn to win and to lose early are better prepared for adult working life
sport should above all remain a source of enjoyment for the children who take part

promptText: Some believe advertising aimed at children should be banned outright. Others argue it teaches them about the marketplace and how to make choices. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The statutory regulation of commercial persuasion directed at children and adolescents.
distractors: The prohibition of all advertising broadcast during children's programming.
The commercial exploitation of young consumers by the food and toy industries.
The influence of screen-based media upon the development of the young.

phases.correct: The case for prohibiting outright every form of commercial messaging aimed at the young.
distractors: The instruction of children in the recognition of persuasive technique.
The restriction of advertising for confectionery and other unhealthy foods.
The regulation of the hours during which commercials may be broadcast.

phases.correct: removing persuasive material from an audience that cannot yet recognise persuasive intent
distractors: supplying early encounters with persuasion that a parent can afterwards discuss
relieving parents of the commercial pressure their children exert upon them
curbing the consumption of the products most heavily promoted to the young

phases.correct: Statutory bans on commercial broadcasting during children's programming in Nordic states.
distractors: Voluntary industry codes under which advertisers undertake not to target the under-twelves.
Restrictions on the advertising of confectionery before the evening broadcast watershed.
School policies forbidding branded merchandise and sponsored teaching materials.

phases.correct: a ban confined to broadcast media is readily circumvented by influencer and in-game promotion
distractors: children below the age of about eight cannot reliably distinguish advertising from programming
children exposed to televised advertising press their parents for the promoted goods with striking persistence
advertising revenue sustains the children's programming that a ban would leave unfunded

phases.correct: The instructive function of advertising in the development of commercial literacy.
distractors: The freedom of manufacturers to communicate with their prospective customers.
The revenue that advertising provides to broadcasters of children's content.
The preparation of the young for a marketplace in which persuasive appeals are unavoidable.

phases.correct: furnishing low-stakes encounters with persuasion that a mediating adult can turn into scepticism
distractors: insulating the young from persuasive material until they are old enough to decode its intent unaided
familiarising children with the range of goods and services available to their households
teaching young consumers to compare price and quality before committing their money

phases.correct: Media-literacy lessons that dissect real campaigns so pupils identify persuasive technique.
distractors: Classroom debates in which pupils design advertisements for products of their own invention.
Advertising-industry workshops delivered in schools by practitioners who explain how campaigns are built.
Household conversations in which parents explain to a child why a televised claim is exaggerated.

phases.correct: children below roughly eight cannot separate advertising from content, so the instructive case fails
distractors: prohibition confined to television is easily evaded through sponsorship and product placement
the critical scepticism supposedly taught by exposure is acquired far more reliably at school
commercial literacy is transmitted by parents and teachers, not by the advertisements a child happens to see

phases.correct: advertising should be barred for the youngest children and permitted later alongside compulsory media-literacy teaching
distractors: advertising should be permitted at every age provided that schools deliver compulsory instruction in persuasive technique
commercial messaging aimed at any person below the age of majority ought to be prohibited entirely
regulators should police the content of children's advertisements rather than restrict the age of the audience

phases.correct: regulation should track cognitive capacity, since harm depends on whether persuasive intent is recognised
distractors: the youngest children require protection because they cannot yet recognise persuasive intent at all
a single statutory age threshold is administratively simpler and therefore preferable to graduated restriction
commercial pressure upon the young has grown far too intense for voluntary codes to restrain it

promptText: Some think it is acceptable for minority languages to disappear if it makes global communication easier. Others believe governments should spend money to keep them alive. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The preservation of endangered languages under pressure from global convergence.
distractors: The emergence of a single dominant language for international scholarship and commerce.
The public cost of sustaining tongues spoken by very small communities.
The relationship between a community's language and its cultural identity.

phases.correct: The acceptance of linguistic consolidation in the interest of communicative efficiency.
distractors: The right of every community to conduct its public affairs in its own tongue.
The practical advantages that a shared international language confers upon trade and research.
The natural attrition of languages as an unremarkable feature of historical change.

phases.correct: lowering the transactional costs that translation and mutual incomprehension impose
distractors: restoring intergenerational transmission through schooling and official recognition
permitting researchers throughout the world to read one another's findings directly
sparing developing states the expense of maintaining administration in several languages

phases.correct: The adoption of a single working language in international scientific publishing and aviation control.
distractors: The teaching of English as a compulsory second subject throughout state schooling.
Multilingual institutions that translate every document into all their official languages.
The spread of a single language across the internet and international broadcasting.

phases.correct: linguistic loss is rarely a neutral efficiency gain, since it accompanies the marginalisation of its speakers
distractors: revitalisation succeeds only where the language retains some practical utility for its speakers
a shared working language has never prevented speakers from retaining their mother tongue
translation technology will shortly render the choice of a working language immaterial

phases.correct: The commitment of public expenditure to the revitalisation of languages facing extinction.
distractors: The documentation of dying languages by linguists before the last speakers are lost.
The obligation of the state to protect the cultural inheritance of its minorities.
The provision of interpreting services for speakers of minority languages.

phases.correct: restoring intergenerational transmission through education, broadcasting and official status
distractors: recording the vocabulary, grammar and oral literature of a tongue before its last speakers are lost
conferring prestige upon a minority tongue so that parents choose to raise children in it
subsidising publishing and the performing arts in languages that lack a commercial market

phases.correct: Immersion schooling and broadcasting quotas that returned Welsh and Māori to daily use.
distractors: Archives of recorded speech compiled by linguists working with the last fluent speakers.
Statutory language commissions empowered to require bilingual signage, services and documentation.
Adult evening classes offered without charge to lapsed speakers of a regional tongue.

phases.correct: revitalisation succeeds only where the language retains genuine economic and social utility
distractors: the disappearance of a language is seldom neutral, since it follows the exclusion of its speakers
official status secures a language on paper while its everyday use continues to contract
public money spent on revival is money withheld from schooling and healthcare for the same community

phases.correct: states should fund revitalisation where a community seeks it, while promoting bilingualism rather than rivalry
distractors: states should fund revitalisation wherever a language is endangered, irrespective of whether its community seeks it
public money should support documentation and archiving rather than attempts to restore everyday use
communities wishing to preserve their language should finance that effort from their own resources

phases.correct: diversity and communicative reach are not exclusive, since individual bilingualism secures both at once
distractors: bilingual education allows a child to acquire a global language without abandoning the local one
language policy should follow the wishes of the speech community rather than the preferences of the state
a language carries knowledge and habits of thought that no translation can fully reproduce

promptText: Some argue children should study only their own country's history to foster national pride. Others believe world history matters more for understanding global affairs. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The proper scope of the history curriculum in compulsory schooling.
distractors: The cultivation of national attachment through the teaching of the domestic past.
The place of the humanities within an increasingly vocational curriculum.
The teaching of contested episodes in a nation's history to the young.

phases.correct: The restriction of historical study to the past of the pupil's own nation.
distractors: The comparative examination of several national histories side by side.
The transmission of a shared civic inheritance to the coming generation of citizens.
The reduction of curriculum content to what can be examined reliably.

phases.correct: constructing a shared civic narrative that anchors identity within familiar institutions
distractors: supplying comparative frameworks through which contemporary conflict becomes intelligible
concentrating limited teaching time upon the material pupils will most readily grasp
grounding pupils in the constitutional history of the institutions under which they will vote

phases.correct: Curricula organised around the constitutional and social development of the home nation.
distractors: Programmes of study tracing the nation's colonial expansion and its consequences for other peoples.
Commemorative lessons constructed around national anniversaries and founding documents.
Local history projects in which pupils research the surviving records of their own town.

phases.correct: a purely national syllabus tends toward the celebratory, leaving pupils unable to judge conduct abroad
distractors: a broad global survey risks superficiality, leaving pupils without secure grounding in any context
national curricula are rewritten by each incoming government, so the account pupils receive shifts with politics
pupils seldom retain much historical detail beyond the examination for which it was originally learned

phases.correct: The prioritisation of global historical literacy over the national past.
distractors: The study of the nation's history within its wider international setting.
The cultivation of tolerance through exposure to unfamiliar cultures.
The preparation of pupils for employment in an interconnected international economy.

phases.correct: equipping pupils with comparative frameworks that render contemporary conflict, migration and trade intelligible
distractors: furnishing a shared narrative that situates pupils within the institutions governing them
exposing the young to civilisations whose achievements the national curriculum tends to ignore
demonstrating that no nation's history can be understood in isolation from its neighbours

phases.correct: Thematic units on empire, decolonisation and industrialisation that explain present geopolitical alignments.
distractors: Comparative studies of revolutions across several countries, taught as one connected unit.
Modules on the history of migration and its long-term effects upon receiving societies.
Wide-ranging surveys of the ancient civilisations of several continents and periods.

phases.correct: a sweeping global survey risks superficiality, leaving pupils with fragmentary impressions and no grounding
distractors: a purely national syllabus becomes celebratory and disguises the country's conduct overseas
world history is difficult to examine fairly because its content resists any settled canon
teachers trained in the national past are seldom equipped to teach global themes convincingly

phases.correct: schools should teach the national past as a case study embedded within wider global processes
distractors: schools should teach national and world history as two separate strands allotted equal curriculum time
the national past should be taught first and the wider world introduced only in the final years
curricula should be determined by teachers rather than prescribed centrally by government

phases.correct: historical causation crosses borders, so a curriculum divided by geography misrepresents the past
distractors: pupils cannot interpret their own nation's history without knowing that of its neighbours
an education system exists to produce informed citizens rather than to cultivate patriotic sentiment
global affairs are now so entangled that a national perspective alone explains very little

promptText: Some think the government should bear the full cost of housing and caring for the elderly. Others believe families should take sole responsibility for their older relatives. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The distribution of responsibility for the care of an ageing population between state and family.
distractors: The escalating cost to the public purse of supporting an ageing population.
The standard of care available to elderly people in residential institutions.
The decline of the multigenerational household in industrialised societies.

phases.correct: The treatment of elderly care as a collective obligation of the state.
distractors: The provision of pensions and medical treatment to citizens beyond the age of retirement.
The professional standard of care that trained institutions are able to provide.
The relief of ordinary families from the financial burden of long-term care.

phases.correct: pooling longevity risk so that no household is bankrupted by a long illness
distractors: preserving continuity of relationship and obligation between the generations
financing trained staff, equipment and premises that no individual family could procure alone
guaranteeing a uniform standard of provision irrespective of a family's income

phases.correct: Universal long-term care insurance funded through general contribution, as in Japan.
distractors: State subsidies paid directly to relatives who care for an elderly person at home.
Publicly funded residential homes admitting all applicants without regard to means.
Statutory entitlements to nursing, respite and domiciliary support administered by local authorities.

phases.correct: fully institutional provision substitutes supervision for relationship, producing security alongside isolation
distractors: responsibility placed wholly upon relatives falls hardest upon women and upon households without the means to absorb it
public provision spares families the ruinous expense that a prolonged final illness would impose
elderly people generally prefer to remain in their own homes rather than enter an institution

phases.correct: The location of caring responsibility exclusively within the family.
distractors: The support of family carers through respite provision and paid leave.
The moral duty owed by adult children to reciprocate the care they themselves received.
The familiarity and comfort of care delivered in a person's own home.

phases.correct: preserving continuity of relationship and reciprocal obligation across the generations
distractors: sparing the taxpayer the expense of institutions that families could staff themselves
keeping older people within familiar surroundings and among the people they know best
transmitting an expectation of care downward, so that each generation learns the obligation in turn

phases.correct: Multigenerational households in which adult children provide daily care alongside employment.
distractors: Adult daughters who reduce their working hours or leave employment entirely to nurse a parent at home.

phases.correct: sole familial responsibility falls disproportionately on women and entrenches existing inequality
distractors: institutional care replaces relationship with supervision, securing the body but isolating the person

phases.correct: the state should guarantee the clinical and financial floor of care while supporting families to sustain the relational element
distractors: the state should meet the entire cost of care while families contribute companionship as they choose
families should provide daily care, with public provision reserved for those who have no relatives
the cost of elderly care should be apportioned between the state and the family in fixed proportion

phases.correct: dignified ageing requires both the material security only collective provision can guarantee and the continuity only families supply
distractors: families alone can supply the affection and continuity of relationship that no institution is able to replicate
the burden of an ageing population has grown far too great for individual households to carry it unaided
public provision is far more efficient and equitable than the uncoordinated efforts of individual families

promptText: Some argue that genetically modified crops are essential to feed a growing population. Others believe they carry serious, unknown dangers to human health and ecosystems. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The role of genetic engineering in securing the global food supply.
distractors: The contribution of agricultural technology to the elimination of world hunger.
The safety of genetically modified produce for regular human consumption.
The control of patented seed stock by multinational agribusiness firms.

phases.correct: The indispensability of engineered crops for feeding an expanding population.
distractors: The conferring of drought tolerance and pest resistance upon staple crops.
The profitability of engineered seed for the agricultural export sector.
The reduction in pesticide application achieved across engineered farmland.

phases.correct: conferring drought tolerance and pest resistance that lift yields on land already farmed
distractors: extending cultivation into regions previously considered too arid to farm
removing the need for irrigation and fertiliser throughout the developing world
shortening the growing season so that several harvests may be taken annually

phases.correct: Vitamin-fortified and salt-tolerant staples grown where conventional varieties fail.
distractors: Hybrid cereals of the Green Revolution that multiplied yields across Asia.
Laboratory trials establishing the nutritional equivalence of engineered grain.
State subsidies encouraging smallholders to adopt patented seed varieties.

phases.correct: hunger arises chiefly from distribution failure and poverty rather than from scarcity
distractors: the objection concerns the pace and ownership of modification rather than the principle
engineered varieties have already raised the yields of staple cereals across several continents

phases.correct: The unquantified hazard posed to human health and to ecological systems.
distractors: The demonstrated toxicity of engineered produce to those who consume it.
The dependence of cultivators upon a small number of seed corporations.
The displacement of inherited agricultural knowledge within farming communities.

phases.correct: releasing novel genetic material into open systems whose effects cannot be recalled

phases.correct: Herbicide-tolerant varieties that have bred resistant weeds and narrowed diversity.

Import prohibitions imposed by states unwilling to accept engineered commodities.

phases.correct: selective breeding has reshaped crop genomes for millennia, so the principle is not new
distractors: yield alone cannot resolve a shortage that is produced by distribution and poverty

the risks commonly cited are hazards of industrial agriculture rather than of modification

phases.correct: states should license engineered crops under independent monitoring while tackling poverty
distractors: engineered crops should be approved wherever independent testing establishes that they are safe to eat
the technology should be suspended until its long-term consequences are fully understood

phases.correct: risk resides in the regulatory and commercial structure, not in modification itself

promptText: Some think public libraries are no longer needed because information is available online. Others believe they play a vital role as community spaces and sources of physical resources. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The continuing function of public libraries in a networked society.

The reading habits of citizens who enjoy unlimited internet access.

phases.correct: The redundancy of the physical library given universal digital access.
distractors: The instant retrieval of catalogues and reference works from anywhere.
The declining number of visitors recorded by municipal branches each year.
The expense of maintaining premises that comparatively few citizens use.

phases.correct: making catalogues and reference works retrievable without premises or opening hours
distractors: digitising collections so that a branch may serve readers far beyond its own district
sparing readers the cost and inconvenience of travelling to a municipal building
allowing an unlimited number of readers to consult one text at once rather than await its return

phases.correct: Open-access repositories consulted by researchers who never enter a reading room.
distractors: Subscription databases that libraries themselves purchase on behalf of their readers.
Encyclopaedias maintained collaboratively and revised continually by their readers.
University reading lists delivered to students entirely in electronic form.

phases.correct: digital sufficiency presupposes connectivity, devices and search literacy, none evenly distributed
distractors: libraries that have not restructured around civic use continue to lose their readers
much scholarly material remains behind paywalls that private individuals cannot afford

phases.correct: The library's role as shared civic infrastructure and guaranteed public space.
distractors: The provision of internet terminals to households without a connection.
The preservation of printed collections that exist in no digital form.
The professional guidance offered to readers by trained reference staff.

phases.correct: supplying a non-commercial space with expert help and equipment few can afford privately

phases.correct: Branches serving as job-search centres, language classrooms and sole internet access.
distractors: Reading rooms kept open late so that students may revise for their examinations.

phases.correct: the civic case justifies the institution rather than its inherited nineteenth-century form
distractors: connectivity, devices and the literacy to search are not evenly distributed across a population

phases.correct: libraries should be funded as civic and digital infrastructure, with lending one service among many
distractors: libraries should modernise their collections so that readers may borrow electronically as well
municipalities should concentrate provision in fewer, larger branches offering a fuller range of services
public reading provision should be transferred to schools and to community associations

phases.correct: access to information depends upon the human infrastructure that makes it usable

promptText: Some argue that personal lifestyle changes are the best way to fight climate change. Others believe only large-scale government action and corporate regulation can work. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The level at which intervention against climate change is most effective.

phases.correct: The primacy of individual behavioural change in the reduction of emissions.

distractors: demonstrating to legislators that an electorate will accept the cost of decarbonisation
reducing the emissions attributable to domestic heating, diet and private travel

phases.correct: The necessity of statutory regulation and of structural reform.

The scale of investment required to rebuild energy and transport systems.

phases.correct: Carbon pricing, grid decarbonisation and efficiency standards that cut national emissions.

phases.correct: regulation of this magnitude is unsustainable without the public consent that visible commitment generates

phases.correct: structural regulation must carry the decisive share, with individual action supplying its mandate
distractors: individuals should change their habits and press their governments to legislate as well

phases.correct: emissions are governed by the systems within which choices are made, not by intention

responsibility should rest with those whose decisions determine what the majority may choose

promptText: Some believe new buildings should be designed in a traditional style to blend with historic surroundings. Others argue that bold, modern architecture should always be encouraged. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

The influence of planning authorities upon the appearance of a city.

promptText: Some argue that raising the minimum wage cuts poverty and strengthens the economy. Others believe it drives businesses to raise prices and shed jobs. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The economic consequences of statutory increases to the wage floor.

phases.correct: transferring income to households that spend it locally, reducing reliance on state subsidy

narrowing the gap between the lowest and the median earnings in a country

additional earnings are spent locally, sustaining the very businesses that pay them out
